data.title: FTSE 100 logs first monthly gain in three; AstraZeneca jumps
data.description:
London's FTSE 100 logged its first monthly gain in three months, edging up on Friday due to a boost from AstraZeneca, with investors welcoming a budget that was softer than expected on taxes.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index CURRENCYCOM:UK100 ended about 0.1% higher at 10,729.78 points, rising over 1% in October. The midcap FTSE 250 slipped nearly 1% on the day.

Here are more details:

  • AstraZeneca jumped 7% in its best day in a year after the Anglo-Swedish drugmaker announced a restructuring drive that will likely save $1.5 billion and help achieve long-term ambitions, including investing in new drug pipelines

  • The broader pharma sector (.FTNMX201030) gained 5.1%, its biggest monthly gain since February

  • Banks (.FTNMX301010) weighed most on the index on Friday after NatWest lost nearly 9% following a weaker-than-expected outlook for interest income

  • Precious and industrial (.FTNMX551020) metal miners lost 5.3% and 2.9%, respectively, tracking declines in gold and copper

  • BP rose 0.5% after posting a record quarterly net profit

  • Earlier this week, finance minister John Healey's first budget raised taxes on banks and gambling firms by less than expected, sparking a rally in the stocks

  • Aerospace and defence firms were among the best performers this week after Healey said that 'reprioritisation' in other departments would fund the government's defence plan

  • Consumer staples stocks rose on the day, with British American Tobacco and Unilever up 1.7% and 2.1%

  • Earlier this month, data showed inflation rose more than expected in September, cementing the case for an interest rate hike by the Bank of England in November

data.title: What Does the Weil Gotshal Implosion Mean for the Law-Firm Industry? — WSJ
data.description:
By Erin Mulvaney and Andrew Scurria

The turmoil at Weil, Gotshal & Manges has led its leaders to wind down the law firm. They took the steps as the firm hemorrhaged top lawyers and had no clear succession plan after its incoming chair declined to step into the role.

As of Friday the would-be chair and a top private equity lawyer, Ramona Nee, was in talks to join Kirkland & Ellis, a massive rival with which Weil had struggled to compete.

Such a fall is extraordinary for a firm with some 1,200 lawyers worldwide and had been among the most well-regarded and profitable in the industry.

Despite its woes, Weil raked in $2.1 billion in revenue last year and, like most law firms, it has relatively few liabilities outside of its global office leases.

Here's what to know about the demise of one of Wall Street's most vaunted law firms and what happens now.

What triggered Weil's misfortunes?

The roots of the crisis at Weil date back more than a decade. The firm raked in business during the chaotic aftermath of the 2008-09 financial crisis but failed to reinvest those profits and even cut lawyers when many of its competitors were in growth mode. It has fallen behind industry leaders in head count, revenue and profit — leaving it vulnerable to poaching from rival firms.

Weil has pushed hard in the past year or so to grow, seeking a firm with which to merge and amping up efforts to lure new partners. Some firm insiders say there was a power struggle between influential partners who wanted to grow to compete with mega-firm rivals and others who wanted to remain smaller. In March, the firm elected private-equity partner Ramona Nee to take over leadership in January 2027. Nee recently decided to walk away from the role.

In September, news broke that Michael Aiello, the firm's top dealmaker, was leaving for Cravath, Swaine & Moore. It marked an inflection point. Efforts soon accelerated to find a merger partner. When a deal with Willkie Farr fell through and more top lawyers announced their departure, confidence in Weil's future cratered.

"A law firm's most valuable asset is its people. If they go home one night and don't come back the next day, it's over," said Albert Togut, a bankruptcy lawyer who handled the infamous collapse of Dewey & LeBoeuf.

What does the dissolution of a huge law firm mean for the industry?

In addition to Nee, many of the firm's partners, including Matt Barr, the head of Weil's prized restructuring practice, are being heavily courted by rivals. Barr is expected to stay at the firm to oversee the wind down. Landing those lucrative practice groups is crucial for firms who are in a race for top talent and scale.

The firm also has hundreds of associates who will be flooding the job market. Hiring at big law firms typically follows a rigid schedule, with firms beginning to interview future associates as early as their first semester of law school and making final hiring decisions before they begin their final year. That creates challenges for the roughly 100 Weil first-year associates looking for jobs outside of that timeline.

The whole legal industry is a bit chaotic right now. What's going on?

The partner exodus at Weil reflects upheaval in the legal industry as firms compete fiercely for top talent. Even healthy firms with strong reputations can be destabilized if they lose key people or practice groups.

It was once unusual for partners to jump from firm to firm, but in the current market, some of the most successful firms have amassed so much money that they can lure partners with $20 million-plus guarantees.

Unlike people in other industries, lawyers aren't bound by noncompete agreements, making lawyers free agents — and when they leave, they often take their prized clients with them.

Why is it shocking that Weil finds itself in crisis?

Weil, a white-shoe firm founded nearly a century ago by Jewish lawyers who were often excluded from other elite shops, has established itself as a blue-chip restructuring powerhouse with a strong record of clinching private equity and M&A deals. The firm was a pioneer in building a restructuring practice, leading some of the largest bankruptcies in history, including those of Lehman Brothers, General Motors and Enron.

Its financial picture has been healthy. Its partners earned $5.6 million each last year, making it one of the top 20 most profitable firms. But while partner profit at the top 100 firms grew 14% last year, Weil's grew only 4%.

How will Weil Gotshal wind down its financial affairs?

While some collapsing law firms have filed for chapter 11, Weil at this point is planning to wind down its affairs without a bankruptcy filing. Even as a shell of its former self, the firm is likely to continue to exist in some form for an extended time to manage the tasks of settling its accounts receivable, dealing with leases at offices around the world and administering payments to employees and partners.

Other firms hobbled by partner defections have wound down without the expense of a bankruptcy proceeding, including the restructuring and transactional boutique Stroock & Stroock & Lavan in 2023. Although Weil's affairs are more complex, the firm enters wind-down in a relatively strong financial position, with few liabilities and no debt. But it isn't clear how much of the firm's outstanding bills it will be able to collect or on what timeline.

This explanatory article may be periodically updated.

data.title: BETA Completes 14 All-Electric Flights Across Florida Under U.S. DOT and FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program
data.description:
BETA Technologies () (“BETA”), an aerospace and defense company, has completed 14 flights across Florida, covering nearly 700 nautical miles, under the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and U.S. Department of Transportation (U.S. DOT) Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) Integration Pilot Program (eIPP). BETA is a partner in Florida’s eIPP project, alongside lead participant Florida Department of Transportation, Republic Airways, Brickyard Connection and Metro Aviation. BETA’s conventional fixed-wing electric aircraft, the ALIA CTOL, has flown across the Orlando and Tampa regions, including routes from St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport (KPIE) and Albert Whitted Airport (KSPG) to Tampa International Airport (KTPA).

“The eIPP lets us fly electric aircraft in the National Airspace System alongside our customers to evaluate how the aircraft perform in real-world operations,” said Kyle Clark, founder and chief executive officer of BETA. “ALIA is all-electric and mechanically simple, so it’s inexpensive to operate and maintain, and we built the charging network in parallel. Florida invested early, and our chargers are now at nine sites from the Panhandle to the Space Coast. Earlier this year, the aircraft and the network together supported high-cadence operations with Republic Airways along the I-4 corridor, up to nine flights a day at under $17 in energy per flight. We’ve logged more than 250,000 nautical miles across our CTOL and VTOL fleet to get here. The eIPP is where we put that experience to work, on the routes our customers will fly in commercial service.”

BETA’s flights from Albert Whitted Airport in St. Petersburg to Tampa International follow the route of the world’s first scheduled commercial airline flight, which Tony Jannus flew in 1914.

“Florida is helping safely integrate these new aircraft into the airspace system and prove that the next great era of American aviation is already here,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “Each flight provides crucial data and lessons learned that will help establish safety standards for everyday operations.”

“More than 100 years ago, Florida helped launch the commercial aviation industry. Today, we are helping shape the next era of flight,” said Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared W. Perdue, P.E. “Through strategic investments, statewide planning, and partnerships with some of the industry’s top innovators, Florida is creating the infrastructure and policies needed to safely integrate Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) into our transportation system. These flights demonstrate how we are turning vision into reality.”

Earlier this year, BETA signed an agreement with the Florida Department of Transportation to supply 34 chargers and thermal management systems. Florida is home to BETA’s largest charging network in the U.S., with chargers currently online at nine sites:

  • Bob Sikes Airport (KCEW)

  • Duke Field (KEGI)

  • Tallahassee International Airport (KTLH)

  • Jacksonville Executive at Craig Airport (KCRG)

  • Gainesville Regional Airport (KGNV)

  • Tampa International Airport (KTPA)

  • SunTrax Advanced Air Mobility Facility

  • Kissimmee Gateway Airport (KISM)

  • Space Coast Regional Airport (KTIX)

BETA’s chargers are multimodal and interoperable, and designed to integrate with existing airport infrastructure. They are UL-certified and use the Combined Charging System (CCS) standard, so any CCS-compliant electric vehicle, in the air or on the ground, can charge at a BETA site.

“We believed in Kyle Clark and his team long before most people understood what electric aviation could mean for our industry,” said Todd Stanberry, vice president and co-owner of Metro Aviation. “What I love about these demonstrations is that we’re not just talking about the possibilities anymore. We’re seeing them happen. Whether it’s moving passengers, cargo or patients, BETA continues to show us why we believed in them from day one.”

BETA’s ALIA family includes the ALIA CTOL and an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft (the ALIA VTOL), built for passenger, cargo, medical, emergency response, and defense missions.

Florida is the host of BETA’s last eIPP kickoff event. BETA is participating in seven of the eight programs selected by the FAA and U.S. DOT, which together span 26 states, including Virginia, Maryland, Louisiana, Texas, North Carolina, Utah, New York, Vermont and now Florida. Across these programs, BETA, its customers and state and local partners are flying electric aircraft in real operating environments, integrating them into the National Airspace System (NAS) and generating the operational data the FAA and U.S. DOT need to shape the rules for safe, routine commercial service.

For photos of BETA’s Florida eIPP operations, please see here.

For more information on BETA’s eIPP operations, please see here.

About BETA Technologies, Inc.

BETA () is an aerospace and defense company designing, manufacturing and selling high-performance electric aircraft, advanced electric propulsion systems, components and charging systems to top operators worldwide. BETA’s intentional approach to developing the enabling technologies necessary to electrify aviation unlocks lucrative aftermarket revenue opportunity over the life of each aircraft. These highly scalable enabling technologies allow BETA to serve a customer base across cargo and logistics, defense, passenger and medical end markets and unlock cost-effective and safe missions. Visit www.beta.team for more information about BETA and its products.

data.title: Walmart and Base Power Announce a Strategic Agreement to Bring Affordable Home Backup Power and Energy Savings to Customers
data.description:
Walmart today announced a strategic investment in Base Power, a Texas-based energy company, along with an agreement that will make Base’s home energy offerings available to Walmart customers and Sam’s Club members – expanding access to affordable energy solutions that can benefit both households and the grid. Base’s home battery systems are designed to help lower energy costs when the grid is on and provide backup power when it’s not.

Beginning in November, customers and members who enroll in an eligible Base home battery offering at participating Walmart and Sam’s Club locations will receive 20% off Base Power’s standard upfront battery installation fee.

More Options for Home Energy

Base Power installs, owns and maintains its home battery systems, with customers paying an upfront installation fee, which is a fraction of the cost of traditional whole-home backup solutions. In eligible areas of Texas, Base also offers electricity plans designed to help customers lower their bills.

“We’ve built Base around a simple idea: families deserve electricity that’s affordable when the grid is working and dependable backup power when it isn’t,” said Zach Dell, CEO of Base Power. “Walmart has been helping Americans save money and live better for more than 60 years. Base brings that same commitment to home energy, and we’re excited to do it together.”

“Customers and members count on Walmart and Sam’s Club to help them make the most of their budgets,” said Shayne Wahlmeier, SVP of Walmart Energy. “Base Power gives them a practical way to help lower energy costs, have backup power during outages and support a more reliable grid. We’re proud to make these solutions more accessible through Walmart and Sam’s Club.”

Starting in Texas

Texas is Base Power's largest and most established market, where Base serves more than 35,000 members. More than 20,000 of those households have a Base battery at home, and the remaining members have their electricity from Base. Walmart is launching these offerings in Texas first and expects to expand to additional locations and markets over time.

Product availability, savings potential, installation requirements and pricing vary by location, utility service area and customer circumstances.

Customers and members can meet with Base representatives at participating Walmart and Sam's Club locations to learn about available services, ask questions and enroll.

About Walmart

Walmart Inc. () is a people-led, tech-powered omnichannel retailer helping people save money and live better - anytime and anywhere - in stores, online, and through their mobile devices. Each week, approximately 280 million customers and members visit more than 10,900 stores and numerous eCommerce websites in 19 countries. With fiscal year 2026 revenue of $713 billion, Walmart employs approximately 2.1 million associates worldwide. Walmart continues to be a leader in sustainability, corporate philanthropy, and employment opportunity. Additional information about Walmart can be found by visiting corporate.walmart.com, on Facebook at facebook.com/walmart, on X at x.com/walmart, and on LinkedIn at linkedin.com/company/walmart.

About Base Power

Founded in 2023 and headquartered in Austin, Texas, Base Power is an energy company building a grid for the future. The company’s mission is to advance human prosperity through energy abundance – delivering reliable and affordable power for all. data.title: Ford CEO Aims for a 20% Sales Jump by 2032 — WSJ
data.description:
By Ryan Felton and Christopher Otts

Ford Motor expects to sell 5 million cars a year by early next decade, Chief Executive Jim Farley told workers this week, a sales volume the company hasn't reached since before the pandemic.

Farley announced the target — a roughly 20% increase over its current volume — in a town hall meeting Thursday, saying Ford aims to reach it by 2032, people familiar with the comments said. He said the company will generate the uptick in sales on the back of several new models in the coming years, the people said.

The company's global strategy turns on Farley's emphasis to no longer make "boring" vehicles, which for now has left it without the budget-friendly small sedans and SUVs it used to give priority to. Farley has said that making affordable vehicles remains a priority, however, and Ford is planning to launch five new models priced below $40,000 by the end of the decade, including an all-electric pickup truck.

The new car market is shrinking, and high interest rates and fuel prices are challenging consumers who are already dealing with average transaction prices around $50,000. At the same time, Ford has been wrestling with stiff competition from Chinese upstarts around the world, a reality that will become more complicated if those companies were to break into the U.S. The company's stock is down about 8.5% for the year.

Ford declined to comment.

Ford has delivered about 3 million vehicles to dealers worldwide through Sept. 30, a 9% decline from the same period in 2025, according to the company. The last time the carmaker eclipsed 5 million in global sales was in 2019, before the pandemic. As recently as a decade ago, the automaker sold over 6 million units a year globally, industry data shows.

Ford's sales decline in recent years has been driven in part by a decision to discontinue several popular, but low-margin models, including the Escape and Edge SUVs, that amounted to hundreds of thousands of sales each year.

The company expects the new $30,000 EV truck, called the Fathom, to generate over 100,000 sales in its first year of production, The Wall Street Journal has reported. The Fathom is on target to begin production in the fourth quarter of 2027, executives said this week.

Overseas, Ford plans to roll out several new vehicles in Europe through partnerships with the French car company Renault and China's Geely, which will build cars together at a Ford factory in Spain.

Valereum Plc

("Valereum", "VLRM" or the "Company")

Resignation of Corporate Adviser

Valereum Plc (AQSE: VLRM | OTCQB: VLRMF), a company aiming to become the global market leader in the tokenised digital markets sector, announces that at 15:07 today, it received notification that Guild Financial Advisory had resigned as Corporate Adviser with immediate effect.

The Company is considering its options and will provide further announcements as appropriate.

The Directors of the Company accept responsibility for the contents of this announcement.

Please visit the Company's website at www.vlrm.com

For more information, and the chance to have your questions directly answered by the management team, please head to our interactive investor hub via: Investor Hub.

IMPORTANT NOTICES

The Company holds cryptocurrencies or crypto assets in its treasury. Whilst the Board of Directors of the Company considers holding cryptocurrencies to be in the best interests of the Company, the Board remains aware that the financial regulator in the UK (the Financial Conduct Authority or FCA) considers investment in cryptocurrencies to be high risk. At the outset, it is important to note that an investment in the Company is not an investment in cryptocurrencies, either directly or by proxy and shareholders will have no direct access to the Company's holdings. However, the Board of Directors consider cryptocurrencies to be an appropriate store of value and potential growth and therefore appropriate for the Company. Accordingly, the Company is and intends to continue to be materially exposed to cryptocurrencies.

The Company is neither authorised nor regulated by the FCA, and the purchase of certain cryptocurrencies are generally unregulated in the UK. As with most other investments, the value of cryptocurrencies can go down as well as up, and therefore the value of the Company's cryptocurrencies holdings can fluctuate. The Company may not be able to realise its cryptocurrencies holdings for the same as it paid to acquire them or even for the value the Company currently ascribes to its cryptocurrencies positions due to market movements. Neither the Company nor investors in the Company's shares are protected by the UK's Financial Ombudsman Service or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

Cryptocurrencies may present special risks to the Company's financial position. These risks include (but are not limited to): (i) the value of cryptocurrencies can be highly volatile, with value dropping as quickly as it can rise. Investors in cryptocurrencies must be prepared to lose all money invested in cryptocurrencies; (ii) the cryptocurrencies market is largely unregulated. There is a risk of losing money due to risks such as cyber-attacks, financial crime and counterparty failure; (iii) the Company may not be able to sell its cryptocurrencies at will. The ability to sell cryptocurrencies depends on various factors, including the supply and demand in the market at the relevant time. Operational failings such as technology outages, cyber-attacks and commingling of funds could cause unwanted delay; and (iv) crypto assets are characterised in some quarters by high degrees of fraud, money laundering and financial crime. Prospective investors in the Company are encouraged to do their own research before investing.

The Company also holds digital tokens as part of its strategy to become the global market leader in the rapidly developing tokenised digital markets sector. Whilst the Board of Directors of the Company considers holding tokens to be in the best interests of the Company, it is important to note that an investment in the Company is not a direct or indirect ownership interest, security, or claim in respect of any underlying asset or reserve to which a token may relate. The valuation of tokens, particularly those linked to mining reserves or other physical assets, is inherently uncertain and may depend on independent third-party verification. Further risks include the liquidity of the tokenised markets, reliance on the security and continued operation of underlying blockchain or smart contract infrastructure, counterparty and custody risk in respect of third party platforms, the risk of misrepresentation or fraud regarding underlying reserves, and evolving regulatory, tax, and accounting treatment. It should not be assumed that tokens carry rights or protections to traditional securities or regulated investment products and investors are encouraged to conduct their own due diligence on the Company's exposure to tokenised assets before making any investment decision.

data.title: Serbia's Russian-owned NIS oil firm secures new US sanctions waiver, state TV reports
data.description:
Serbia's Russian-owned NIS oil company has secured a new waiver against US sanctions until December 11, state RTS TV reported on Friday.

A previous waiver by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) expires on Friday.

The new one will allow NIS, which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to continue importing crude oil until the sale of a Russian majority stake in the company to Hungarian energy company MOL .

OFAC imposed sanctions on NIS in October 2025 as part of wider measures targeting Russia's energy sector over the war in Ukraine.

It has since extended a series of waivers for NIS to allow for the divestment of the combined 56% stake held by Russia's Gazprom Neft and Gazprom in the company.

NIS imports oil primarily from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Nigeria, Guyana, Norway, the US, Libya and Iraq.

The company covers around 80% of market demand in Serbia, where a leaderless student-led protest movement unseated longtime leader Aleksandar Vucicin in elections last Sunday, heralding a new era in the Balkan country.
